newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadians work long hours in Q1, StatsCan says.
newsitem.headline: Canadians work long hours in Q1, StatsCan says.

text.p: Almost one fifth of all Canadian employees worked overtime during the first quarter of 1997, the majority of them for no extra pay.
Statistics Canada said on Monday that about six out 10 employees working overtime were not paid for their extra work.

Those who did not get paid for their overtime worked an average of 9.2 extra hours during their regular work week, while those who were paid overtime worked an average of 8.5 hours a week, the federal agency said.
Adult men were twice as likely as women to get paid for their overtime. And white-collar workers were more likely than blue-collar workers to have put in extra hours, Statistics Canada said.
The agency also found that despite recent strength in job creation in Canada, a significant number of people are still working part-time involuntarily.

In the first three months of 1997, about six percent of part-timers were involuntary, or about 852,000 people. But the number of underemployed workers -- involuntary part-time workers who actually looked for full-time work -- was about 293,000 or about two percent of the work force, StatsCan said.
Young Canadians were more prone to underemployment than adults, the agency said.

StatsCan also detected a growing tendency for Canadians to hold more than one job, especially part-time workers. In 1996, about one in five Canadian workers held more than one job compared to one in 50 two decades earlier.
The fastest growing group of multiple job holders was women aged 25 to 54, StatsCan said.
